paragraphs.heading: What oscillation is
paragraphs.text: Oscillation is a repeating, back-and-forth change in some quantity, usually over time, around a central value or between two or more states. The central value is often a point of equilibrium, a resting balance. A swinging pendulum and alternating current are familiar cases. A mechanical oscillation is called a vibration, and physicists also use oscillations to approximate complex interactions, such as those between atoms.

paragraphs.heading: A weight on a spring
paragraphs.text: The simplest mechanical example is a weight on a linear spring, acted on only by its weight and the spring's tension; an air table or ice surface comes close to this. When the spring is still, the system is at equilibrium. Pull the weight aside and a restoring force pushes it back toward equilibrium. By the time it gets there it has picked up momentum, so it overshoots, and a new restoring force builds the other way.

paragraphs.heading: Energy trading places
paragraphs.text: The swinging carries on because energy keeps changing form. As the mass passes equilibrium it has kinetic energy, and at the far ends of its path that energy is stored as potential energy in the spring. When the restoring force is directly proportional to the displacement, the regular motion is called simple harmonic motion. The time one oscillation takes is often called its period.

paragraphs.heading: Frequency, amplitude, phase
paragraphs.text: The motion is described by its frequency ω, its amplitude A and a phase shift δ. All three are set by how the system starts out. With no friction, the spring and mass would swing between plus and minus the amplitude forever.

paragraphs.heading: Why swings fade
paragraphs.text: Every real oscillator is thermodynamically irreversible. Friction, electrical resistance and similar processes keep turning some of its stored energy into heat. So oscillations tend to die away unless energy keeps flowing in. With β as the damping coefficient and ω₀ as the natural frequency, damped oscillators fall into three groups. An oscillator is under-damped when β is smaller than ω₀, over-damped when β is larger, and critically damped when the two are equal.

paragraphs.heading: Driving and resonance
paragraphs.text: An oscillator can also be pushed by an outside force, for example an AC circuit hooked up to a power supply outside it; the oscillation is then called driven. Resonance happens in a damped, driven oscillator when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, ω = ω₀. At that point the amplitude of the swings is as large as it can be.

paragraphs.heading: Flutter in a wing
paragraphs.text: Some systems draw energy from their surroundings, usually when they sit in a flowing fluid. Flutter in aircraft wings is an example. A tiny displacement of the wing raises its angle of attack and its lift coefficient, which pushes it still further. At large enough displacements, the wing's stiffness takes over as the restoring force and an oscillation results.

paragraphs.heading: Two directions at once
paragraphs.text: In an anisotropic oscillator the restoring force differs by direction, so each direction has its own frequency. If one frequency is twice the other, the path traces a figure eight. If the ratio of the frequencies is irrational, the motion is quasiperiodic: periodic along each axis, yet it never repeats as a whole.
